book.title: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!
book.author: Richard P. Feynman and Ralph Leighton

confidence_note: Well-known episode from the book (Cornell cafeteria plate), recalled; not page-checked. Omitted as unverified: the colleague's name and exact words, the exact wording of the Nobel remark, the date, Cornell department details. Wobble-to-spin ratio stated as the medallion turning about twice for each wobble. Bethe name and ratio caveat from search results (Physics Today letter by Sidney Coleman, 1988).
facts: After the war Feynman was at Cornell and felt burned out; physics no longer gave him pleasure and he felt he could not produce.
He decided to play with physics, whatever interested him, without caring about importance.
In the cafeteria a student tossed a plate into the air; it wobbled and the Cornell medallion on it turned.
Feynman noticed that the medallion turned faster than the wobble, about twice as fast.
He worked out the equations for the wobbling plate for fun, and a colleague asked what the use of it was; he said it had none.
Working on the plate led him to think about electron behavior, which led to the work he later received the Nobel Prize for.
A colleague, Hans Bethe in Feynman's telling, asked what the importance of it was; Feynman said it had none and he was doing it for fun.
Feynman writes that the work he later got the Nobel Prize for came from that wobbling plate. A later physicist's letter notes the ratio is the reverse of the one he stated.
scene_details: a plate tossed into the air in the cafeteria
the red Cornell medallion turning twice per wobble
a colleague asking what it was good for
tension: A burned-out physicist works on the one problem that has no use.
opening_idea: Open on the plate spinning above a cafeteria table.

lessons.idea: Work started only for the fun of understanding can restore the energy that duty has drained.
lessons.anchor: the plate was useless; it led back to electrons

reflect_final: What small problem at work or home would you pick up for no reason except that it interests you, and when could you give it an hour?

use_cases.situation: Your team is stuck and tired on a deliverable.
use_cases.move: Say a physicist once restarted by working out why a plate wobbles, and propose an hour on a side question that interests people.

use_cases.situation: A friend feels drained by their job.
use_cases.move: Ask what small puzzle they used to enjoy and when they last did it.

use_cases.situation: You postpone a hobby because it serves no purpose.
use_cases.move: Block one hour this weekend for it with no goal.

pocket_idea: Feynman, burned out, worked out why a tossed plate wobbles for no reason, and that led back to his Nobel work. Give a useless puzzle an hour.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Feynman got his love of physics back by working out why a plate wobbles when it is tossed in a cafeteria.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Burned out at Cornell, Feynman decided to play with physics. In the cafeteria a plate wobbled in the air, its medallion turning twice per wobble. He worked out the equations for fun, and that led him back to electron work that won the Nobel.
